question: How many public holidays are observed nationwide across Switzerland, and which one is it?

options.A: Exactly one — 1 August, Swiss National Day
options.B: Two — 1 January (New Year's Day) and 1 August (Swiss National Day)
options.C: Three — 1 January, 1 May (Labour Day) and 1 August (Swiss National Day)
options.D: None — Switzerland has no nationwide public holidays at all; each canton sets its own calendar entirely

source_quote: The first of August – Swiss national day – is Switzerland's only national public holiday.
notes: Distinctive because 1 January, Easter Monday, Ascension Day and 1 May are statutory holidays in neighbouring EU states but carry no nationwide status in Switzerland. The cantonal layer is covered separately in K082.

question: Beyond Switzerland's single nationwide public holiday, what is the maximum number of additional public holidays a canton may declare on its own territory?

options.A: Up to two
options.B: Up to four
options.C: Up to eight
options.D: Unlimited

source_quote: The cantons can each have up to eight additional public holidays on their territory. Public holidays can thus vary from canton to canton.
notes: CANTONAL-VARIABLE — the holiday calendar differs by canton and within a canton by commune. Framed as a cantonal power, not a federal rule.

question: In Switzerland, a public holiday falls during an employee's annual leave. How is that day treated?

options.A: It counts against the employee's vacation entitlement, so the employee effectively loses one day of leave
options.B: It must be added to the following year's leave entitlement
options.C: It is compensated with a wage supplement of at least 25%
options.D: It does not count as a day of vacation

source_quote: If a public holiday falls during your vacation, that day does not count as a day of vacation.
notes: Distractor A is the German rule, where public holidays falling inside the leave period reduce the annual leave entitlement. Deliberate German/Austrian-import trap.

question: What is the general rule under Swiss law on working on a Sunday?

options.A: Sunday work is freely permitted for any employee who has consented to it
options.B: Sunday work is generally prohibited, and is possible only subject to a special authorisation and the employee's consent
options.C: Sunday work is generally prohibited, but a simple notification to the employer is sufficient to make it lawful
options.D: Sunday work is generally prohibited and can never be authorised, in any sector

source_quote: Working on Sundays is generally prohibited in Switzerland. However, working on Sundays is possible, subject to special authorisation and the employee's consent.
notes: D is false: the health sector, hospitality, newsstands and bakeries, theatres, cinemas and the media may work Sundays without authorisation.

question: Between which hours of the day is work prohibited by the Swiss night-work ban?
source_quote: In Switzerland, the law prohibits work between 11pm and 6am.
notes: Note the source spells the window as 11pm to 6am. No national maximum weekly working time is stated on the source pages and none is asserted here.

question: Under Swiss law, what is the maximum number of hours a night worker may work in any 10-hour period, counting breaks?

options.A: 8 hours
options.B: 10 hours
options.C: 9 hours
options.D: 11 hours

source_quote: Night workers may not work for more than 9 hours in any 10-hour period, including breaks.
notes: Unusual as a rule: the maximum is expressed as a ceiling inside a rolling window rather than as a daily hour total.

question: In Switzerland, what is the minimum daily rest period an employer must grant to an employee aged 20 or over between two working days?

options.A: 8 hours
options.B: 11 consecutive hours
options.C: 12 hours
options.D: 10 hours

source_quote: it must last at least 11 consecutive hours
notes: Distractor C is the rule for employees under 18 ('the daily rest period must always be at least 12 hours'); distractor A is the once-a-week reduction the employer may grant if the two-week average is 11 hours.

question: An employee works between 11pm and 6am on fewer than 25 nights per calendar year. What must the employer pay for those nights?

options.A: Time off equal to 10% of the night hours worked
options.B: A wage supplement of at least 10%
options.C: A wage supplement of at least 50%
options.D: A wage supplement of at least 25%

source_quote: A supplement of at least 25% must be paid for work between 11pm and 6am carried out for less than 25 nights per calendar year.
notes: Distractor A is the regime for regular night work (25 or more nights per calendar year), where the compensation is time off equal to 10% of night hours; distractor C is the 50% supplement for occasional Sunday work. Cash payment in lieu of compensatory time off is prohibited.

question: Under Swiss law, which authority must an employer approach to obtain authorisation to employ workers for occasional night work?

options.A: The competent cantonal authority
options.B: The State Secretariat for Economic Affairs (SECO)
options.C: The Federal Office for Customs and Border Security (FOCBS)
options.D: The commune in which the workplace is situated

source_quote: To employ workers for occasional night work, employers must contact the competent cantonal authority to apply for authorisation.
notes: Distractor B is correct only for authorisations for regular Sunday work, which go to SECO — the cantonal/federal competence split is the point being tested.

question: In Switzerland, which level of government is responsible for compulsory education?

options.A: The Confederation, acting through a federal education ministry
options.B: The communes, which set the school system and appoint the teachers
options.C: The cantons
options.D: The cantons jointly with the Confederation, under federal supervision

source_quote: Compulsory education is the responsibility of the cantons. This is why it is important to check the information on your canton's website.
notes: Switzerland has no federal school system — the structural opposite of Germany, Austria and France. Distractor B is scope confusion: communes run individual schools, but the responsibility statement sits with the cantons.

question: How many years of compulsory schooling do children in most Swiss cantons have to attend, and how is that total made up?

options.A: 9 years in total: 7 years of primary school followed by 2 years of secondary school
options.B: 11 years in total, including the two years of kindergarten
options.C: 11 years in total: 9 years of primary school followed by 2 years of secondary school
options.D: 13 years in total: 11 years of primary school followed by 2 years of secondary school

source_quote: In most cantons, children are required to attend school for 11 years, including the two years they attend kindergarten.
notes: CANTONAL-VARIABLE in the details. Distractor C keeps the total but wrongly moves the two kindergarten years out of primary school.

question: How is compulsory schooling normally split between primary and secondary level in Switzerland, and which canton departs from that pattern?

options.A: Eight years of primary school including kindergarten and three years of secondary; Ticino instead has seven years of primary and four years of secondary
options.B: Six years of primary and five years of secondary; Ticino instead has five years of primary and six years of secondary
options.C: Nine years of primary and two years of secondary; Ticino instead has eight years of primary and three years of secondary
options.D: Eight years of primary and three years of secondary; Ticino follows the same 8+3 split as the other cantons

source_quote: Primary school, including kindergarten, usually comprises eight years. Secondary education usually comprises three years. In Ticino, primary school lasts seven years and secondary school four years.
notes: CANTONAL-VARIABLE — 8+3 is the usual structure and is NOT a federal rule; naming Ticino is required to keep the question unambiguous.

question: Kindergarten in Switzerland generally starts at age four, with an enrolment deadline that is usually 31 July. What does the official guidance say about that deadline?

options.A: The deadline of 31 July applies in every canton without exception
options.B: The deadline is set nationally at 15 September
options.C: The deadline is set by each individual school, so it varies from school to school within every canton
options.D: Some cantons in eastern and central Switzerland have a different cut-off date

source_quote: Some cantons in eastern and central Switzerland have a different cut-off date.
notes: CANTONAL-VARIABLE — 'most children' start at four, but the entry cut-off is not uniform. A model asserting a single national school-start rule has imported a foreign assumption.

question: Which three parties share responsibility for maintaining standards in the Swiss vocational education and training (VET) system and for ensuring an adequate number of apprenticeship places?

options.A: The Confederation, the cantons and the trade unions
options.B: The Confederation, the Cantons and professional organisations
options.C: The Confederation, the cantons and the chambers of commerce and industry
options.D: The cantons, the communes and the professional organisations

source_quote: The Confederation, the Cantons and professional organisations all contribute to maintaining the high standard of vocational education and training and strive to ensure that there is an adequate number of apprenticeship positions available.
notes: Distractor C is the German model (IHK/HWK chambers); there is no chamber tier in Swiss VET. Distractor D drops the Confederation, a deliberate scope-confusion.

question: In the Swiss VET system, which qualification follows from which programme length?

options.A: A two-year programme leads to a Federal VET Diploma; three- and four-year programmes lead to a Federal VET Certificate
options.B: A two-year programme leads to a specialised school certificate; three- and four-year programmes lead to a specialised baccalaureate
options.C: A two-year programme leads to a Federal VET Certificate; three- and four-year programmes lead to a Federal VET Diploma
options.D: Two-, three- and four-year VET programmes all lead to the same Federal VET Diploma

source_quote: Two-year VET programmes lead to the award of a Federal VET Certificate; three-year and four-year VET programmes lead to the award of a Federal VET Diploma.
notes: Distractor B belongs to the separate specialised-school route (three-year certificate, then a one-year specialised baccalaureate), which is easy to conflate with VET.

question: Roughly what share of young people in Switzerland takes the dual vocational education and training route rather than an academic upper-secondary school?

options.A: About one in four
options.B: About one in two
options.C: About three in four
options.D: About two in three

source_quote: Two-thirds of young people in Switzerland benefit from the solid foundation provided by vocational education and training.
notes: Distractor B mirrors the German apprenticeship uptake of roughly one in two. The Swiss dual-route share is markedly higher.

question: Switzerland recycles a high share of its waste, yet materials recovered from waste form only a small share of the country's total material consumption. What are the two figures?

options.A: 70% of total waste volume recycled, but secondary raw materials at 14% of total material consumption
options.B: 70% of total waste volume recycled, and secondary raw materials at 70% of total material consumption
options.C: 14% of total waste volume recycled, and secondary raw materials at 70% of total material consumption
options.D: 53% of municipal solid waste recycled, and secondary raw materials at 14% of total material consumption

source_quote: At present, over two thirds (70%) of Switzerland's total waste volume is recycled. Measured against total material consumption, materials recovered from waste (known as secondary raw materials) make up only a small proportion: 14% in 2019
notes: The 14% figure is from 2019; the 70% recycling rate is 'at present' as published by FOEN. Distractor D uses the municipal-solid-waste rate (53% in 2020), which measures a different quantity. MUNICIPAL-WASTE-VARIABLE: municipal waste figures are administered at commune level.

question: According to the Federal Office for the Environment, which of these four materials had the highest recycling rate in Switzerland in 2020?

options.A: Aluminium
options.B: PET
options.C: Glass
options.D: Paper

source_quote: Recycling focuses on established materials such as glass (recycling rate in 2020: 99%), PET (recycling rate in 2020: 82%), aluminium (recycling rate in 2020: 97%), paper (recycling rate in 2020: 82%).
notes: The published rates are glass 99%, aluminium 97%, PET 82% and paper 82%. The top two are only two points apart, so intuition about 'metal vs glass' is not sufficient — the exact figures are required.

question: A traveller returning to Switzerland carries goods for personal use with a total value of CHF 400. The tax-free import limit is CHF 150. On what amount is the Swiss import VAT calculated?

options.A: On the excess only — the CHF 250 by which the total value exceeds the CHF 150 limit
options.B: On the whole value — CHF 400
options.C: On the first CHF 150 only
options.D: On nothing, because all the goods are for personal use

source_quote: If the total value exceeds CHF 150, you must pay VAT on the total value of the imported goods. Example: The total value is CHF 400.
notes: Distractor A is the intuitive 'excess only' rule used in many other countries. The verified Swiss tax-free limit is CHF 150 per person per day.

question: What are the Swiss standard VAT rate and the reduced rate that applies to goods such as foodstuffs, books, magazines and medicines?

options.A: 6.7% standard, 2.1% reduced
options.B: 8.1% standard, 3.8% reduced
options.C: 10.0% standard, 2.6% reduced
options.D: 8.1% standard, 2.6% reduced

source_quote: VAT is 8.1%. A reduced rate of 2.6% applies for certain goods (e.g. foodstuffs, including non-alcoholic beverages, books, magazines and medicines).
notes: Distractor A is the pre-2001 Swiss rate pair. Figures as published by the Federal Office for Customs and Border Security at access date 2026-10-12.

question: A restaurant guest asks whether they must leave a tip in Switzerland. What is the correct position according to the national tourism organisation's own statement of local custom?

options.A: The guest is not obliged to tip, although paying a tip is customary in many restaurants.
options.B: Tipping is compulsory in restaurants, and the amount is fixed at ten percent of the bill by federal regulation.
options.C: Tipping is compulsory only in Zurich and Geneva, and optional everywhere else in the country.
options.D: The guest is obliged to tip whenever the restaurant has more than five employees.

source_quote: In Switzerland, the guest is not obliged to tip. In many restaurants, however, it is customary to pay a tip.
notes: Swiss-specific: customary but not a legal obligation. Distractors invent a federal fixed rate and cantonal differences that do not exist.

question: Where a guest does leave a tip in a Swiss restaurant, what does the national tourism organisation describe as the customary amount?

options.A: A flat five francs per person, regardless of the size of the bill.
options.B: Approximately ten percent of the bill, or a round-up to a round figure.
options.C: Exactly fifteen percent, which is the rate used throughout the EU for hospitality services.
options.D: Whatever the guest decides, with no commonly recognised convention at all.

source_quote: This amounts to approximately 10 percent or it is rounded up to a round amount.
notes: Picks the convention up from the same sentence. C imports an EU-style rate; D denies the stated convention.

question: Why is tipping optional in the Swiss hospitality sector, according to the report's account of the industry?

options.A: Because service is already included in the price in that sector, so a tip is a bonus rather than payment for the service itself.
options.B: Because Swiss law forbids employers from paying staff out of a tip pool.
options.C: Because tipping was abolished in Switzerland by the federal government in 1974.
options.D: Because restaurants in Switzerland are required to include a service charge instead of accepting tips.

source_quote: The catering industry is one of those sectors in which service is actually included in the price. Nevertheless, some customers add a tip when paying for good service.
notes: The causal link models miss: optional because service is priced in. C misreads 'since 1974' as an abolition date.

question: Under the rules in force when the report was published, how were voluntary tips treated for tax and social security purposes?

options.A: Voluntary tips were always fully taxable as ordinary salary income, with no exceptions.
options.B: Voluntary tips were generally exempt from tax and contributions, but a tip forming an integral part of an employee's salary was treated as income and became subject to tax and social security deductions.
options.C: Voluntary tips were exempt from income tax but always subject to social security contributions.
options.D: Voluntary tips fell outside the scope of Swiss tax and social security law altogether, in every circumstance.

source_quote: Under current rules, voluntary tips are generally exempt from tax and contributions. However, if a tip forms an integral part of an employee's salary, it is treated as income and is therefore subject to tax and social security deductions.
notes: Conditional structure matters: exemption is the general rule, not absolute. D is the over-generalised version.

question: A lawyer asks how the phrase 'a substantial part of salary' is defined in Swiss law for the purpose of taxing tips. What does the reporting identify?

options.A: It is defined numerically as any amount above CHF 20 per month.
options.B: It is defined in the Federal Act on old-age and Survivors' Insurance.
options.C: The law does not clearly define it, which the report characterises as a source of legal uncertainty.
options.D: Each canton defines it individually, so the threshold differs canton by canton.

source_quote: The law does not clearly define what constitutes a "substantial part" of salary.
notes: Tests resistance to inventing a precise threshold for an undefined statutory term. B is a plausible-looking but wrong statute.

question: In a Swiss restaurant that shares tips among staff, how is the sharing governed, according to the hospitality trade association's own statement?

options.A: By a federal collective agreement that sets one fixed percentage for all staff.
options.B: By the canton, which issues a binding allocation formula for tip pools.
options.C: By the collective agreement, which requires tips to be paid out in proportion to hours worked.
options.D: There are no generally applicable rules; operational practice differs from establishment to establishment.

source_quote: In manchen Restaurants werden die Trinkgelder unter den Mitarbeitenden aufgeteilt. Allgemein gültige Regelungen gibt es nicht, die betriebliche Praxis ist unterschiedlich.
notes: Evidence quote is the association's German original; question is the harvester's translation. A/C/D each posit a binding mechanism the source denies.

question: The hospitality trade association states that tips are not wages. How should that statement be weighted when answering a question about Swiss law?

options.A: It is settled Swiss law, because the trade association is the sector's competent authority.
options.B: It is settled Swiss law, because it is written into the hospitality sector's collective agreement.
options.C: It carries no weight at all, because a trade association has no standing to interpret employment law.
options.D: It is the association's own position and is contested by labour-law academics, so it cannot be presented as settled law.

source_quote: Grundsätzlich sind Trinkgelder kein Lohn und auch kein Bestandteil davon. Das Gastgewerbe verfügt über einen guten Landes-Gesamtarbeitsvertrag.
notes: A source-criticism item: the answer is about evidential weight. B is the trap - the collective agreement exists but does not settle the point.

question: As of the report's publication in March 2026, who was expected to decide whether tips become fully subject to social security contributions?

options.A: The cantonal governments, which vary the rule by canton.
options.B: The Federal Council, acting alone, as it does for all tax questions.
options.C: Parliament, following a proposal intended mainly to close social security coverage gaps.
options.D: The cantonal tax authorities, which already have discretion to set the threshold.

source_quote: Whether tips should remain tax-free or become fully subject to contributions will now be decided by parliament.
notes: Distinguishes proposing from deciding. C is the common error: assuming the executive settles tax treatment unilaterally.

question: A traveller returning to Switzerland carries goods intended for personal use with a total value of CHF 140. What does the Swiss VAT tax-free limit imply for these goods?

options.A: They may be imported VAT-free.
options.B: VAT at the standard rate of 8.1% is due on the whole value.
options.C: VAT at the reduced rate of 2.6% is due on the whole value.
options.D: Customs duties must be paid on them in addition to VAT.

source_quote: When you return from abroad or enter Switzerland, goods up to a total value of CHF 150 may be imported VAT-free (tax-free limit), provided they are intended for your personal use or as gifts.
notes: The threshold is CHF 150, not the CHF 100 used by a number of other jurisdictions, and it is a VAT threshold rather than a duty-free allowance - so the duty distractor is wrong at this value.

question: How often may the CHF 150 tax-free limit be claimed by a traveller entering Switzerland on the same day?

options.A: Once per family per day, with a child's own claim only from age six
options.B: Once per person per day, children included
options.C: Once per person per week, so a second crossing on the same day adds nothing
options.D: Once per day for each adult, with a separate claim for each accompanying child

source_quote: The tax-free limit can be claimed only once per person and per day. It applies also for children.
notes: Traps the assumption that the allowance is per group or per week, and the assumption that a child's own goods consume a separate claim - the children's allowance is part of the same per-person, per-day claim.

question: A Swiss resident buys goods abroad purely for resale in a Swiss shop and brings them back. How are those goods treated at import?

options.A: They are covered by the CHF 150 tax-free limit in the same way as any other purchase made abroad
options.B: They are covered by the tax-free limit as long as their total value stays below CHF 150
options.C: They are subject to VAT
options.D: They are subject to VAT only if their total value exceeds CHF 150

source_quote: Goods that are not intended for your personal use or as gifts are subject to VAT.
notes: The allowance tests purpose first and value second; commercial goods fall outside it at any value. Distractor D is the common confusion of treating value as the only test.

question: Which of the following is not counted when a traveller works out whether the CHF 150 tax-free limit is exceeded?

options.A: Duty-free foodstuffs bought in the aircraft's duty-free shop
options.B: Tobacco products and alcoholic beverages carried in from abroad
options.C: Repairs or maintenance work carried out abroad on the traveller's own private vehicle
options.D: The traveller's personal effects and the fuel put into their vehicle

source_quote: The value of personal effects, travelling provisions and fuel for your vehicle is not included.
notes: Personal effects, travelling provisions and fuel are excluded, whereas duty-free foodstuffs, tobacco, alcohol, household pets and work done abroad on the private vehicle all count towards the limit. The trap is transferring the duty-free-shop exemption from customs duty to the VAT threshold.

question: A traveller returns with goods that stay below the CHF 150 VAT tax-free limit but exceed the duty-free allowances for alcohol. What is still payable?

options.A: Customs duties
options.B: VAT at the standard rate of 8.1%
options.C: Customs duties and VAT at the reduced rate of 2.6%
options.D: Nothing further, because the CHF 150 limit covers all import charges

source_quote: In addition to VAT, you must pay customs duties if the goods you are carrying exceed the duty-free allowances for alcohol, tobacco products and certain foodstuffs.
notes: The CHF 150 figure is the VAT tax-free limit; the separate duty-free allowances belong to customs duties. Distractor C mixes the two regimes and adds a rate that does not apply to alcohol.

question: A traveller receives a gift abroad and declares it to Swiss customs. On what basis is the import VAT assessed for such a gift?

options.A: On any receipt the giver can produce, or else on a self-declared value
options.B: Its market value
options.C: On the nominal value printed on the gift packaging, where one exists
options.D: On the recipient's own estimate of what the gift is worth to them personally

source_quote: Otherwise, the market value is taxed, e.g. in the case of gifts. The market value refers to the sum a third party would have had to pay to buy the item.
notes: Purchases are taxed on the invoice, receipt or purchase contract; where there is none - gifts in particular - the market value applies, i.e. what a third party would have paid. Traps are the self-declared value and the recipient's sentimental valuation.

question: Roughly how much waste does Switzerland generate in a year, according to the Federal Office for the Environment?

options.A: About 8 to 9 million tonnes
options.B: About 30 million tonnes
options.C: About 80 to 90 million tonnes
options.D: About 300 million tonnes

source_quote: Overall, Switzerland generates about 80 to 90 million tonnes of waste annually, and it is fair to assume that the total quantity will continue to rise in the future.
notes: Order-of-magnitude anchor for the whole waste topic: the headline recycling rate makes Swiss volumes sound modest, but construction and demolition account for the great majority. Distractors straddle the correct figure by roughly a decade each.

question: Which activity generates the largest share of Switzerland's total waste volume?

options.A: Households, offices and small businesses through municipal solid waste collection
options.B: Demolition of buildings, roads and railway lines
options.C: Special treatment of hazardous waste
options.D: Excavated and quarried materials from construction activity

source_quote: The largest share of waste in Switzerland is generated by construction activity: excavated and quarried materials comprise just under two thirds of all waste (57 million tonnes), and a fifth of the waste stems from the demolition of buildings, roads and railway lines (17 million tonnes).
notes: Municipal solid waste is only about 7% of the total, so the intuition imported from EU or US waste debates - that household waste dominates - inverts the Swiss picture. Demolition is large but smaller than excavation.

question: Under the Swiss Waste Ordinance, from when must phosphorus be recovered from sewage sludge, animal and bone meal and reused?

options.A: 1 January 2026
options.B: 1 January 2016, the year the Waste Ordinance was enacted
options.C: 1 January 2036, once the transition period granted by the Federal Council has run
options.D: 1 January 2021, five years after the Ordinance was enacted

source_quote: In that year, Switzerland became the first country in the world to make it obligatory to recover the nutrient phosphorus: from 1 January 2026, phosphorus has been recovered from sewage sludge, animal and bone meal and reused in agriculture or the chemical industry. The Federal Council has granted the cantons and the business community a 10-year period of grace.
notes: Three dates are in play and are easy to interleave: the Ordinance and first-country claim date from 2016, the obligation bites from 1 January 2026, and a 10-year grace period runs for the cantons and industry.

question: On which principle is the financing of waste disposal in Switzerland based?

options.A: Waste disposal is financed from general federal tax revenue collected centrally
options.B: The 'polluter pays' principle
options.C: The cantons and communes must cover the full cost of disposal from their own budgets
options.D: Producers of packaged goods finance disposal through a federal levy on packaging

source_quote: The disposal of all waste costs Switzerland a good CHF 3 billion a year. The 'polluter pays' principle is widely applied in Switzerland, i.e. whoever creates the waste must also pay for its disposal.
notes: The named principle matters more than the CHF 3 billion figure: whoever creates the waste pays for its disposal. Traps are the centrally funded reading and the producer-llevy model, neither of which is the stated basis.

question: In 2020, approximately how much hazardous waste underwent special treatment in Switzerland or was exported for environmentally sustainable disposal?

options.A: About 1.85 million tonnes, all of it exported for disposal abroad
options.B: About 0.5 million tonnes
options.C: About 1.85 million tonnes
options.D: About 7 million tonnes

source_quote: In 2020, approximately 1.85 million tonnes of hazardous waste underwent special treatment in Switzerland or was exported for environmentally sustainable disposal under strictly monitored conditions (0.5 million tonnes).
notes: The 0.5 million tonnes is the export subset inside the 1.85 million tonne total, so the two figures are routinely swapped. The distractor at 7 million tonnes reflects confusing hazardous waste with the hazardous fraction of municipal waste.

question: Roughly how many professions can a young person in Switzerland choose from when looking for an apprenticeship?

options.A: About 24
options.B: About 140
options.C: About 2,400
options.D: Over 240

source_quote: How do I find an apprenticeship? In a first step, you can choose from over 240 professions. Then look for a company with an opening for an apprenticeship.
notes: The two nearest confusions are the order-of-magnitude errors 24 and 2,400; the distractors are chosen so that a model guessing a plausible Swiss-sounding number still lands wrong.

question: In the Swiss dual apprenticeship, where does an apprentice normally acquire the practical part of the training and the theoretical basics of the profession?

options.A: In the host company and at the vocational school respectively
options.B: At the vocational school for both, with the host company supplying only workspace and materials
options.C: In the host company for both, with the vocational school offering only optional exam preparation
options.D: Split between the host company and a branch training centre run by the professional organisation

source_quote: In most cases, your host company will provide you with practical training and you will learn the theoretical basics of your profession at the vocational school. In some cases, you can also complete your apprenticeship full-time in a school.
notes: The dual model with company practice and school theory; the page also notes the minority full-time school-based route. Distractor B is the German-style reading where the vocational school is the main provider, and D imports a third mandatory venue.

question: What does the Swiss academic baccalaureate qualify its holder to study, and how long does the programme normally take?

options.A: Study at a university or a federal institute of technology, on a four-year programme
options.B: Study at a university of applied sciences, on a three-year programme
options.C: Study at a university or a federal institute of technology, on a two-year programme
options.D: Study at a teacher training college only, on a six-year programme

source_quote: You usually start baccalaureate school after the second or third year of upper-secondary level school. The study programme lasts four years in most cantons and aims to provide a good general education. Students do not learn a profession, however the completion of an academic baccalaureate gives them access to study at a university or a federal institute of technology (ETH Zurich or EPFL).
notes: Separates the academic baccalaureate (general education, access to university and the ETH/EPFL) from the vocational baccalaureate (access to a university of applied sciences) and from the specialised school route, which is three years plus one.

question: In Switzerland, admission to a baccalaureate school depends on which factor?

options.A: The Confederation alone, under a uniform federal admission rule
options.B: The commune alone, through a single entrance test for all cantons
options.C: The canton and the type of baccalaureate
options.D: The federal institute of technology the pupil intends to attend afterwards

source_quote: If you want to study for a baccalaureate, you need to meet different requirements depending on the canton and the type of baccalaureate you wish to obtain, including good grades, a recommendation from your class teacher or a successful entrance examination.
notes: Entry is cantonal and type-dependent: good grades, a class teacher's recommendation or an entrance examination. Traps are the assumption of a single federal rule and the assumption that grades alone decide.

question: In which month does the Swiss school year generally begin?

options.A: September
options.B: July
options.C: January
options.D: August

source_quote: The school year starts in August.
notes: Anchors the point that the school calendar is set cantonally and communally rather than by federal law - the exact holiday dates come from the commune or the school itself. September is the default imported from neighbouring systems.

question: Under Swiss rules, who is responsible for getting a child to school, and when may a commune step in?

options.A: The parents, with commune support only where the route is very long or too dangerous
options.B: The commune, which must provide transport for any child living more than two kilometres from school
options.C: The canton, which arranges school transport for every child in its territory
options.D: The parents, with commune transport guaranteed for any child of compulsory-school age

source_quote: Getting a child to school is the responsibility of the parents. The communes only provide support if the route to school is very long or too dangerous.
notes: Communes step in only for a very long or dangerous route, which is what Pedibus-style schemes address. The over-general distractor D sounds like a parental duty with municipal backing and is the trap for those who half-remember the rule.

question: Which authority in Switzerland sets the rules and conditions for homeschooling a child of compulsory-school age?

options.A: The Confederation, which sets a single national home-education ordinance
options.B: The canton, which sets its own rules and conditions
options.C: The commune, which must first approve the arrangement in writing
options.D: The school itself, which may refuse the arrangement only on academic grounds

source_quote: Children can be sent to a public school or they can be homeschooled. Contact your canton for the specific rules and conditions.
notes: Homeschooling is possible in Switzerland but the conditions are cantonal - there is no federal home-education ordinance. The federal-ordinance reading is imported from Germany, where a Bundesland ordinance framework exists.

question: Under Swiss law, how much time off may an employee take for a special event such as a marriage or the birth of a child?

options.A: A fixed entitlement of one day per event is guaranteed throughout Switzerland
options.B: A fixed entitlement of three days per event applies in every canton
options.C: The employer sets the rules
options.D: A statutory half-day per event applies in cantons that adopted the model rules

source_quote: The law does not clearly define how many hours or days you can take off. Ask your employer about the rules that apply in your company.
notes: The duration of these special absences is not fixed by law, unlike the minimum vacation entitlement, which is. The trap is confusing the two and assuming a uniform statutory day count for special absences.

question: A cantonal public holiday falls on a Saturday, which is a non-working day for the employee. How is that holiday treated?

options.A: It is added to the employee's vacation entitlement for that year
options.B: It is compensated with one day of time off during the same week
options.C: It is compensated with a day of time off in the following week
options.D: It cannot be redeemed

source_quote: If a public holiday falls on a non-working day, such as a Saturday or Sunday, you cannot redeem the holiday time during the week.
notes: No time in lieu for a holiday landing on a non-working day - a real gap in Swiss employment law compared with systems that credit the day. Must not be conflated with the separate rule that a holiday falling during annual leave does not consume a vacation day.

question: Under Swiss rules, how often may an employer shorten the daily rest period below the eleven-hour minimum, and on what condition?

options.A: Once a week, if the two-week average daily rest is 11 hours
options.B: Once a week, at the employer's discretion and without any further condition
options.C: Up to three times a week, provided the two-week average daily rest is 11 hours
options.D: Never for employees aged 18 or over, whatever the two-week average

source_quote: Once a week, your employer has the right to reduce the rest period to 8 hours but only if you have been given an average daily rest period of 11 hours over two weeks.
notes: The eleven-hour daily rest is the baseline; the statutory exception is a single weekly reduction to eight hours, conditional on an eleven-hour average across the two weeks. Traps are unconditional weekly discretion, a higher frequency, and reading the exception as a flat ban.

question: An employer has an employee work between 11pm and 6am on 30 nights in a calendar year. What must the employer provide?

options.A: A wage supplement of at least 25% on top of the hourly wage
options.B: Time off equal to 10% of the night hours worked
options.C: Time off equal to 25% of the night hours worked, or cash in its place
options.D: One rest day of 24 consecutive hours for every ten nights worked

source_quote: Time off equal to 10% of the hours of night work performed must be provided for night work carried out on 25 or more nights per calendar year.
notes: 25 nights per calendar year is the dividing line: below it a supplement of at least 25% is payable, at or above it the employer owes compensatory time off of 10% of the night hours, and paying cash in lieu of that rest is against the law. Distractor D borrows the Sunday-work 24-hour rest figure.
